steps.observation: Work on this for 10 seconds; do not stop early. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The storm had been building all afternoon, a low grumble under the skin of the sea. By dusk the horizon had vanished entirely, swallowed by a curtain of rain and slate-gray cloud. To the north, jagged teeth of rock waited just beneath the surface, invisible even on a clear day. Tonight, they were death in hiding.

Daniel climbed the iron stair that wound up the spine of the lighthouse, one hand on the railing, the other cupped around the little brass watch in his pocket. It had belonged to his father, who had stood this same watch on this same island, and to his grandfather before that. The watch had stopped years ago, but he carried it anyway, a small, stubborn heartbeat of memory.

Halfway up, the tower shuddered as another wave slammed the base. The sound was a hollow, booming roar that echoed up the stone cylinder. The old glass panes rattled in their frames. Daniel paused, steadying himself, and listened. It wasn’t the storm he was listening for—storms were familiar companions—but for those other sounds that sometimes slipped through the howl of wind: the crack of breaking hull, the faint, panicked shout, the flare of a distress rocket.

There was nothing—only the rumble of surf and the climbing whistle of the gale.

At the top, the lantern room glowed with a pale, steady light. The great lens sat like a glass cathedral, its many faces catching and bending the lamplight into a single, white blade that swept the darkness in measured, patient arcs. Daniel stepped into the room, closing the hatch behind him, and checked the clock on the wall. Power had been flickering all evening; he trusted the lens more than the wiring.

He made a slow circuit of the room, hands moving with practiced ease. He checked the backup generator, the fuel, the radio. He wiped condensation from the inner glass and peered out into the night. The sea was a heaving black plain, streaked with white where the waves tore themselves apart. Now and then the lightning showed him the outline of the distant headland, and the taller crests of waves rearing up like creatures trying to climb out of the water.

He could not see the mainland. On clear days he could make out the far-off village: a crooked line of roofs, the suggestion of a road, the faint glitter of car lights. Tonight, the world ended at the edge of his glass.

The beam turned, slow and unfailing. Every ten seconds it reached the same point in its circle—a quiet promise to anyone out there: you are not alone; the rocks are here; the way is there.

The radio crackled at his elbow.

“Harbor Station to Graypoint Light, come in, Graypoint.” The voice was threaded with static.

Daniel lifted the receiver. “Graypoint here.”

“Storm’s worse than expected. We’ve got a trawler overdue from the Banks. Last contact put her five miles east of you, maybe closer now. Keep an eye out.”

Daniel looked toward the east, where the wind drove sheets of rain against the glass. “Copy. I’ll watch for her.”

“Harbor out.”

He set the receiver down and watched the beam swing across the water. Somewhere out there, a boat was fighting this weather with steel and diesel and the stubborn refusal of men who’d been told all their lives that the sea fed them and could therefore be forgiven its moods.

He remembered the first time his father had taken him up into the lantern room during a storm. He had been twelve, thin as a ship’s mast and twice as anxious, clutching the railing as the tower pitched under him.

“Listen,” his father had said, pointing into the furious dark. “This is what we’re for. Not the sunny days. Anyone can find their own way in sunshine.”

Another roll of thunder dragged him back. Daniel moved to the logbook, where the pen lay waiting. 20:47 – storm intensified. Visibility poor. Beam functioning. He wrote neatly, precisely. A record mattered. In the morning, if anything had happened, someone would need to know when and how.

Time thinned into routine, measured by the revolving flash of light, the hum of the generator, the rise and fall of the wind. He adjusted the lens speed once when the motor stuttered, nudged it back into rhythm. He boiled water on the small stove in the corner and drank tea that tasted faintly of rust. Outside, the weather spoke in every language it knew: the drum of rain, the shriek of gusts around the tower, the boom of waves against rock.

Then, just as he turned to refill his cup, he saw it.

A flicker. Not the blind white of lightning, not the steady sweep of his own light. This was a brief, desperate blink of orange somewhere low on the water, east by southeast. A flare, or someone trying to make one.

He set the cup down, already forgotten, and pressed his face to the glass. Another wave of rain surged over the panes, obscuring everything. He wiped a sleeve across the condensation, heart pounding. The lens passed, its light momentarily dazzling him, and in the after-image he almost missed the second flash.

There. Closer now. Definitely a flare, jittery and brief, as if the person holding it was barely managing to keep it above the waves.

Daniel reached for the radio. “Harbor, this is Graypoint. I have visual—possible distress flare east by southeast, approximately three miles. Conditions very poor.”

Static swallowed his words for a moment, then the harbor master’s voice returned, strained. “Copy that, Graypoint. Coast Guard cutter is an hour out, minimum. Can’t launch from here in this surf. You’re our eyes.”

An hour. Daniel set the radio down carefully, as if rough handling might make that number change. He looked again. No more flares, only blackness and water and the amnesiac sweep of rain.

He could not go out. The island was a ring of slippery rock smothered in foam; even in daylight, at low tide, the paths were treacherous. In this? Leaving the tower would only add another name to whatever list the storm was writing tonight.

Inside the lantern room, the machinery ticked and turned. The beam swept. Another ten seconds, another promise. There were times the job felt like a long conversation with emptiness, but not tonight. Tonight, the emptiness was listening back.

Daniel moved to the control box and increased the rotation speed slightly, tightening the beam’s heartbeat. Instead of ten seconds, ships would see the flash every eight, then every seven. It was a small difference, but if the trawler was off course and searching for him, he wanted his presence to be impossible to miss.

He switched on the foghorn, though there was no fog—only the roaring rain. The horn’s bellow rolled out over the sea at regular intervals, another sound for desperate ears to follow.

Minutes blurred as he tracked invisible coordinates in his head: wind direction, estimated drift, tide. He marked them in the log without thinking, though there was no one here to check his math. The notebook began to fill with short, clipped entries.

21:02 – second flare, now lost. Increased rotation speed.

21:11 – no visual. Foghorn engaged. Seas worsening.

He found himself speaking aloud, an old habit. “Come on. You know where I am. I’m right here.”

In his mind they were close enough to see the beam, close enough to feel the vibration of the horn through the hull, but he knew the sea had its own logic. Even a mile away could be too far in this.

Another flash. This time it was close—so close that the light bounced off the underside of the low clouds. He could not see the boat itself, only the brief crown of fire-laced smoke. Then the beam swept past, and for a sliver of a second, he caught it: a dark, pitching outline, bow rising and slamming down, a smear of white letters on the wheelhouse.

He grabbed the binoculars and pressed them to his eyes, but in the time it took to focus, the boat had vanished again into the trough between waves.

Daniel exhaled slowly, as if that might slow the storm itself, and then called harbor again with his updated sighting. The reply was the same: hold on, keep watch, help is coming.

So he did the only thing he could. He kept the light turning, precise and sure. He adjusted the horn and marked the last known position. He watched the darkness as if he could will the trawler toward him with nothing but stubborn attention.

The hours stretched. Once, long after the last flare, he thought he saw a shape too regular to be a wave, but the lightning did not come in time to confirm it. He imagined men on that soaked deck counting the seconds between flashes, cursing and praying and promising to change their lives if only the rocks would stay where he warned them they were.

Sometime past midnight, the storm began to tire. The wind, while still fierce, lost its sharpest edge. The rain thickened into a steady downpour rather than a sideways assault. The thunder wandered away inland, grumbling.

In the early gray before dawn, a voice crackled through the radio.

“Graypoint, this is Coast Guard Cutter Bracken. We’re at your one-eight-zero, half a mile off. We’ve got them.”

Daniel closed his eyes for a moment, bracing a hand on the window frame. “All aboard?” he asked.

“Affirmative. Rough, but all aboard.” A brief pause, then, more softly, “They said they kept sight of your light the whole time. Would’ve been on the rocks without it.”

He looked out at the softening horizon, where the first pale ribbon of morning bled into the clouds. The cutter was a dark smudge, the rescued trawler a smaller, limping shape beside it. Already the sea was smoothing itself out, covering its tracks.

“Glad you found them,” Daniel said.

“Couldn’t have without you. Bracken out.”

He hung the receiver on its hook and turned back to the room. The lens continued its patient rotation, though its flash looked weaker in the coming daylight. He adjusted the settings back to their normal interval, the ten-second heartbeat restored. The foghorn fell silent. In an hour he would make his report, send it in with the details: times, bearings, conditions. The record would show a near-miss, a rescue, a line item on a ledger that rarely saw names.

For now, he added a final entry to the night’s page.

03:12 – CG Cutter Bracken recovered trawler. All hands saved. Light maintained throughout.

He closed the logbook and rested his hand on the worn cover. The tower felt suddenly very quiet, the kind of quiet that comes not from the absence of sound but from the knowledge that something has just passed through and moved on.

Down below, the sea rolled and sighed against the shore, exhausted. Gull cries began, thin and petulant in the thinning rain. On the mainland, in a village he could not yet see, people would be waking to the news that their fathers and sons and friends were coming home after all.

Daniel stood at the window and watched the cutter and trawler crawl toward that unseen harbor. The beam swung past him, briefly washing his reflection from the glass. In its place, for an instant, he saw his father’s face, and behind it the suggestion of another, older still, all of them standing in this same circle of glass and light, listening to the same sea.

The moment passed. The light moved on. Day broke fully, thinning the beam until it was only a pale ghost against the sky.

He descended the iron stair, his footsteps echoing in the empty shaft, and stepped out into the raw, salt-tinged morning. The lighthouse behind him kept its endless vigil, turning and turning, a bright, quiet promise at the edge of the world.
